extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / natural philosophers and experimental scientists (readers of Philosophical Transactions)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reporting empirical experimental observations and explanations (chemical, physical, and natural-history experiments) for publication in a learned society journal. Emphasises detailed method, observable effects, comparative arguments, and witnessable demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors influencing ignition of oils
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing 'ponderous' (heavier) and 'light' (ethereal) oils: ponderous oils require a much greater degree of fire in distillation, often unite more igneous particles, and may contribute to more constant accension; animal oils require greater heat to distil, pass over more volatile salts, sink in water, and tend to continue flame longer though less fiercely than vegetable oils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report specific properties (degree of fire required in distillation, presence/amount of volatile salts, specific gravity/sinking in water) when assessing an oil's tendency to ignite; contrast animal versus vegetable oils and note how distillation conditions affect ignition propensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-of-addition and vacuum effects in reactive mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental outcome depends on the order in which reagents are combined and on atmospheric conditions: e.g., mixing oil of carui-seeds with compound spirit of nitre in a receiver evacuated of air caused an instant explosion and produced enough air to blow up the glass; spirit of wine gives a flash with compound spirit of nitre depending on which is added to which.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record order of combination, whether the experiment was done in air or vacuum, and any immediate effervescence/explosion; compare results when reversing order and note surprising departures from prior expectations (e.g., flame occurring in vacuo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare to known standards (e.g., gunpowder) when characterising new reactive mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare new mixtures to established substances: the 'fiery mixture' and gunpowder both heat, burn, flame and agitate/expand air and can raise bodies opposing them, but differ in that gunpowder will not explode in vacuo and requires actual fire to accension, whereas the fluid mixture produced explosion and flame even in vacuo and by mere mixing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known standards to highlight both similarities and critical differences (conditions for ignition, requirement for prior fire, behavior in vacuo, composition dryness) to clarify the novelty or hazard of a mixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report properties of combustion residue (caput mortuum)
rubrics_metrics.description: After extinction of the flame from the mixture one obtains a light, blackish, spongy, and perfectly insipid substance ('caput mortuum')—sometimes swelling into large protuberances, insoluble by water or common corrosive menstruums, tasting like paper/ashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the residue's bulk, complexion, texture, solubility, and sensory properties (if safe), and note variations with different oils; record whether residue melts in air or dissolves in common solvents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and test order-dependent effervescence (spirit of wine vs spirit of nitre)
rubrics_metrics.description: If spirit of wine is put to the nitre a great effervescence ensues immediately; if spirit of nitre is put on spirit of wine, there may be no ebullition for some time—contrary to other oil experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly test and report asymmetric outcomes when reagents are swapped, and interpret such asymmetries relative to material causes (e.g., volatility, affinity, presence of water).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timber quality indicators: rings, pipes, and growth rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Age is determined by number of rings seen when cut across; the fewer large open pipes present, the stronger the timber. Trees that grow fast (in warm countries) produce closer, tougher timber; slow-growing oaks (e.g., Riga/Dantzic) may be spongy and brittle. Sudden rotting often proceeds from inward/heart decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing timber strength, report ring counts, size and multiplicity of 'large open pipes' (vessels), growth rate and provenance (country/soil), and inspect for heart-decay before felling; specify whether timber was felled in winter/summer and note that differences may be limited to bark and outer rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of Jupiter satellite eclipses for longitude determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Eclipses of Jupiter's first satellite are almost instantaneous and (with good telescopes) discernible near opposition, providing very accurate longitudes—potentially better than lunar methods—provided portable telescopes suffice and charts of coasts are accurately laid down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess astronomical methods on accuracy and practicability: specify instrument requirements (telescopes portable/shipboard), necessity of pre-existing accurate coastal charts, and which satellites (e.g., third vs first) are observable at sea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting the species of magnet pole (tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to find whether an end of iron is north or south: pass the iron through cork/wood and let it swim on water (slow); hold the iron perpendicular and test attraction under the north end of a needle; best: hold the upper end to see if it attracts the needle's south end, since attraction is more sensible than repulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple tests and prefer the more sensitive attraction test with a magnetic needle; note the slowness and potential insensitivity of the floating-on-cork method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and distinction: mutable pole vs fixed pole
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'mutable pole' may be north or south according to how it is held; a 'fixed pole' does not change with orientation (a fixed north pole attracts the needle's south end even when held upwards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State definitions clearly and use them to classify experimental results; record how pole behaviour changes with manipulation or treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing fixed poles by heating and directional cooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat the end (or rod) red-hot and cool the ignited end northward to produce a fixed north pole, or cool it southward to produce a fixed south pole. This method works only for rods of suitable length and diameter: short/thick rods may not acquire fixed poles by ignition, whereas longer or thinner rods can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report rod dimensions (length and diameter), heating thoroughness, and cooling direction when claiming to produce a fixed pole; document failures and threshold lengths/diameters observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignition thoroughness and (lack of) importance of quenching
rubrics_metrics.description: One thorough ignition is more effective than many weak ones; quenching in water does not significantly affect production or hindrance of magnetism, though multiple ignitions may purify iron and accidentally promote magnetism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure thorough ignition (red-hot throughout the treated region); note that repeated quick ignitions are not necessarily superior; record whether quenching was used and its observed effect (often none).

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing poles by hammering, filing, grinding, drilling
rubrics_metrics.description: Hammering (or filing, grinding, drilling, hard or soft rubbing) while the rod is held northward can produce a fixed north pole; success depends on rod length and diameter—there is a minimum length for a given thickness. Heavier blows tend to produce stronger magnetism; a few hard blows can be as effective as many light blows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the mechanical treatment (hammer blows, filing, drilling), the orientation while working (northward/southward), and the dimensions of the rod; report whether the treated end becomes fixed or mutable and the relative strength of magnetism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetry and length-diameter dependence of fixed vs mutable poles
rubrics_metrics.description: Making one end a fixed pole often consequentially renders the other end a fixed opposite pole, but if the rod is sufficiently long relative to thickness, one end can be fixed while the other remains mutable; increasing length can eventually allow both ends to be fixed (even both north or both south) depending on thickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document how changes in length at constant diameter (or changes in diameter) change whether one or both ends become fixed or mutable; report experiments that show thresholds and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loadstone (lodestone) effects depend on rod geometry and strength of the lodestone
rubrics_metrics.description: A loadstone will not make a fixed pole in any iron unless the iron has proper length relative to thickness; a weak loadstone requires greater length; a strong loadstone requires less length to fix a pole, and loadstones may fix poles in thin ends but not in thick ends of the same object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a loadstone, report its relative strength and the rod's length/diameter; record which end acquires polarity and limitations observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longevity of polarity correlates with strength and storage conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger polarity endures longer; weak fixed poles may degenerate to mutable poles in minutes or days when exposed to air or held in a contrary position. Needles touched with good loadstones retain polarity much longer if kept from air and in a meridional position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the observed duration of produced magnetism, storage/orientation conditions, and any decay into mutable poles; include comparisons between loadstone-treated needles and hammer/ignition-treated rods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even when fixed poles cannot be produced, magnetism may be detectable
rubrics_metrics.description: When ignition, hammering, or loadstone contact cannot produce fixed poles for certain rods, there may still be discernible effects of magnetism in them by other tests, though not sufficient to make fixed poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply sensitive tests (needle attraction, other magnetometers) to detect weaker magnetism even when fixed poles are not formed; report these subtle effects rather than claiming no effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical reporting practice: witnessable demonstration and counts in cure/observation reports
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming cures or animal/biological observations (e.g., removal of worms from the tongue), present specimens to spectators, give counts and timings (e.g., 'in less than 8 days took out more than 100 worms'), and cite witnesses of good note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide live/observable specimens or clear physical evidence, quantify findings (numbers, times), and name or describe reputable witnesses to strengthen credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report local remedies and observed environmental effects with contextual detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Local practitioners reported that great noises (horns, drums) repel the 'fiery exhalation' from houses or barns, and that the phenomenon occurred with certain regularity (e.g., one night a week). Location (sandy and marshy), proximity (coming over part of the sea), and effects on cattle should be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting environmental or agricultural phenomena, include location, frequency, local mitigations used, and specific effects on animals or property; report testimony from local observers and note geographical particulars.
